HOW TO LIVE BETTER

How To Live Better

Read the concise How To Live Better guide online: 34 chapters and 640 suggestions about health, safety, money and everyday choices. Use the chapter directory, search and evidence filters to find relevant topics; you do not need to read in order or act on every suggestion.

34 life topics · 640 suggestions · Concise edition

How to read and understand evidence

Find a relevant topic, examine the evidence and costs, and choose one or two actions that fit your situation. Cost-effectiveness includes money, time and energy; these cannot simply be combined into one score.

A: specific figures can be checked. B: research support with limits in the figures or applicability. C: experience and common practice. These are the author's grades; even A-rated entries may be disputed and are not suitable for everyone.

This English translation preserves the PDF's titles, key points, evidence grades and dispute notes. Ellipses mark omissions in the concise original; follow each source for full conditions, explanations and references. Many legal provisions, benefits, yuan amounts and helplines concern China. Translation does not change that jurisdiction. Check original sources and current local rules for medical, legal and policy matters.

Chapter 01

Avoid an early death

This chapter covers fatal accidents and injuries such as traffic crashes, fires and poisoning; a few vaccines and screening tests with particularly strong evidence; and symptoms worth getting checked. The benefit figures come from randomized trials, long-term studies following large populations, or official statistics.

38 matching suggestions

01-01Evidence A

Wear a seat belt in both front and rear seats

Wearing a front-seat belt roughly halves the risk of being killed in a crash; in the front of a light truck, the reduction is about 60%. Among people who died in US vehicles in 2022 whose belt use was known, half were not…

Explanation & sources ↗
01-02Evidence A

Wear and fasten a helmet on motorcycles and electric bicycles

A properly fastened helmet reduces a motorcyclist's risk of death in a crash by about 40%, and head injuries by about 70%. Tighten the strap; a helmet resting loosely on your head does not count.

Explanation & sources ↗
01-03Evidence B

Install smoke alarms; add a carbon monoxide alarm when using indoor coal or gas heating

A working smoke alarm can reduce the risk of death in a house fire by about 60%. Around 40% of people are asleep when a fire starts; smell alone will not wake them reliably.

Explanation & sources ↗
01-04Evidence A

Replace expired gas hoses and stoves; do not alter pipes yourself, and you may refuse gas-company sales pitches

A compliant hose costs tens of yuan. Replacing it when due is a user obligation under China's Urban Gas Management Regulations. Altering pipes or removing gas meters yourself is expressly prohibited.

Explanation & sources ↗
01-05Evidence A

Do not pick, buy or eat wild mushrooms; folk identification methods are unreliable

In 2025 alone, China recorded 828 mushroom-poisoning incidents, affecting 2,165 people and killing 13. Another 34 previously unrecorded poisonous mushroom species were identified that year.

Explanation & sources ↗
01-06Evidence A

Keep electric bicycles out of corridors and elevators; do not charge them at home

Taking electric bicycles into corridors or elevators, or charging them at home, is expressly prohibited by China's fire-safety regulations for high-rise residential buildings.

Explanation & sources ↗
01-07Evidence A

Measure your blood pressure; if it is high, use medication to reach the target

Each 10 mmHg reduction in blood pressure reduces major cardiovascular events by about 20%, stroke by 27%, heart failure by 28%, and mortality by 13%.

Explanation & sources ↗
01-08Evidence A

If overweight after age 35, check fasting glucose and repeat every three years even if normal

A blood test costing tens of yuan can identify prediabetes before symptoms appear. The US official screening recommendation covers overweight or obese adults aged 35 to 70.

Explanation & sources ↗
01-09Evidence B

Do not speed or drive after drinking

Each 1% increase in average speed raises the risk of a fatal crash by about 4%. There is no safe threshold at which a little alcohol is harmless; risk starts rising even at low blood-alcohol levels.

Explanation & sources ↗
01-10Evidence A

Use a child car seat for children under four; do not hold them in your arms

Car seats reduce fatal injury risk by about 70% for infants under one and about 50% for children aged one to four. Holding a child offers no comparable protection; you cannot hold on during sudden braking.

Explanation & sources ↗
01-11Evidence B

Fit window and balcony restrictors when children live at home; insect screens are not safety barriers

A pair of restrictors costs tens of yuan. After New York City supplied high-risk households with free window guards and education, reported child falls in one district halved over three years.

Explanation & sources ↗
01-12Evidence A

Keep children near water in sight; wear life jackets when boating or swimming in open water

People wearing a life jacket when they fall into water have roughly half the drowning risk. Drowning remains the leading cause of death for children aged one to 14 in China.

Explanation & sources ↗
01-13Evidence A

After age 60, train balance and leg strength and make bathrooms and stairs safer

Balance exercises such as tai chi two or three times a week reduce falls by about 23% and the number of people who fall by 15%. Non-slip surfaces and handrails at home can reduce falls by another roughly 20%.

Explanation & sources ↗
01-14Evidence A

Get a hepatitis B marker panel and vaccinate if you lack antibodies

Testing costs tens of yuan. In the 30-year Qidong trial, people vaccinated at birth had an 84% lower risk of primary liver cancer and a lower prevalence of hepatitis B infection…

Explanation & sources ↗
01-15Evidence B

Get nail punctures, splinters or soil-contaminated wounds treated that day; ask about tetanus vaccination

Once tetanus develops, about one in ten patients dies. Deep and soil-contaminated wounds carry the greatest risk. A dirty wound with at least five years since the last dose calls for a booster.

Explanation & sources ↗
01-16Evidence A

Women should get the HPV vaccine as early as possible

In data on 1.67 million Swedish women, those vaccinated before age 17 later had about one eighth the risk of invasive cervical cancer compared with those not vaccinated.

Explanation & sources ↗
01-17Evidence A

Start breast-cancer screening at 40 with a mammogram every two years

Mammography every two years for women aged 40 to 74 is expressly recommended in US official screening guidance.

Explanation & sources ↗
01-18Evidence A

Women over 30 should screen for cervical cancer, preferably with HPV testing

In a rural Indian trial, women who had just one lifetime HPV test had roughly half the risk of dying from cervical cancer and about 50% less late-stage cervical cancer.

Explanation & sources ↗
01-19Evidence A

Start colorectal-cancer screening at 45 to 50, using a fecal immunochemical test or colonoscopy

A stool blood test costing tens of yuan every one or two years reduces colorectal-cancer mortality by about 16%; among those screened at least once, the reduction was 25%.

Explanation & sources ↗
01-20Evidence A

People with cardiovascular disease and older adults should get a flu vaccine every year

In a trial of vaccination after a heart attack, one-year mortality fell from 4.9% to 2.9%.

Explanation & sources ↗
01-21Evidence A

Get the shingles vaccine after age 50

In phase-three trials, the vaccine prevented 97% of shingles cases, with similar results across age groups. The drawback is two doses costing 3,000 to 4,000 yuan out of pocket. That buys a 97% reduction in incidence.

Explanation & sources ↗
01-22Evidence A

Get the pneumococcal vaccine after age 65

In a trial of 84,500 older adults, the 13-valent pneumococcal vaccine prevented about 46% of pneumonia caused by covered strains and 75% of the most dangerous invasive infections.

Explanation & sources ↗
01-23Evidence A

Test for Helicobacter pylori and eradicate it if positive

In a 22-year trial in Linqu, Shandong, people whose H. pylori was eradicated later had roughly half the risk of stomach cancer and about 40% lower stomach-cancer mortality.

Explanation & sources ↗
01-24Evidence A

Heavy smokers should have an annual low-dose chest CT

Eligible heavy smokers receiving annual low-dose CT had 20% lower lung-cancer mortality and 6.7% lower overall mortality than those receiving chest X-rays alone.

Explanation & sources ↗
01-25Evidence B

For depression or suicidal thoughts, call China's 12356 helpline; do not stockpile sleeping pills or pesticides

Evidence for removing lethal means is growing: restricting painkillers reduced related suicides by 43%; installing barriers at common jumping locations reduced them by 86%.

Explanation & sources ↗
01-26Evidence B

Keep a fire extinguisher, fire blanket, escape respirator and first-aid kit; check them yearly

All four are on China's Ministry of Emergency Management list of 11 household emergency supplies. A set costs a few hundred yuan and is a one-time purchase.

Explanation & sources ↗
01-27Evidence B

Get visible blood in urine checked, even if painless or gone the next day

After one episode of visible blood in urine, around 2.8% of people over 60 were ultimately diagnosed with bladder cancer; among those aged 40 to 59, the figure was about 1.2%.

Explanation & sources ↗
01-28Evidence A

If erectile function changes, check cardiovascular health rather than treating it as only a sexual issue

Men with erectile dysfunction later have about 40% more cardiovascular disease and 60% more heart attacks. The difference is greater in younger men. This problem often appears before chest pain.

Explanation & sources ↗
01-29Evidence A

Losing weight, quitting smoking and controlling blood pressure and glucose can improve erectile function

Managing cardiovascular risk factors can improve erectile function itself. Average questionnaire scores rise by two to three points; the scale totals 25, with scores of 22 or above considered normal.

Explanation & sources ↗
01-30Evidence A

Use condoms throughout sex and never share needles

Consistent condom use reduces heterosexual HIV transmission by more than about 70%. Using them most of the time offers little improvement over not using them. They also protect against syphilis and gonorrhea.

Explanation & sources ↗
01-31Evidence A

After high-risk exposure, get an HIV test; China's CDC services offer free, confidential testing

HIV testing at China's disease-control centers is free. National testing rules prohibit staff from disclosing your name, address or test results.

Explanation & sources ↗
01-32Evidence B

Tell someone nearby as soon as suicidal thoughts arise; let them help you through the next few minutes

Nearly half of people who survived a suicide attempt reported no more than ten minutes between the thought and the act. Often the immediate challenge is getting through those few tens of minutes.

Explanation & sources ↗
01-33Evidence B

Do not count on being rescued: emergency care after pesticide or gas poisoning may save life but not lungs or brain

Paraquat has no antidote, and more than 40% of those who ingest it cannot be saved. It inflames and progressively scars the lungs, with kidney and liver damage as well.

Explanation & sources ↗
01-34Evidence B

Do not gamble on recovering quickly after a fall: most trauma-ICU patients survive, but recovery can take years

Only 5.5% of people admitted to a trauma ICU after falling from a height died, but injuries were severe and treatment prolonged.

Explanation & sources ↗
01-35Evidence A

Do not sell a kidney assuming one is enough: the remaining one does double duty, and 86% of sellers reported worse health

Among carefully screened, formally monitored kidney donors, 31 per 10,000 developed end-stage kidney disease over 15 years, compared with four per 10,000 equally healthy non-donors.

Explanation & sources ↗
01-36Evidence A

Do not collect, dismantle or sell unidentified metal objects; stay away from the radiation trefoil symbol

Radiation has no smell, color or temperature. Many radioactive sources look like ordinary pieces of metal, so looking harmless is not a reliable test.

Explanation & sources ↗
01-37Evidence B

If gambling leads to borrowing and persistent low mood, call China's 12356 helpline and let family manage bank cards and payment passwords

People treated in hospital for gambling problems had 15 times the suicide mortality of their peers and 1.8 times overall mortality. Depression was a warning signal for subsequent suicide.

Explanation & sources ↗
01-38Evidence A

Men who have high-risk sex with men should ask an HIV clinic about PrEP; consistent use cuts infection by over 70%

Pre-exposure prophylaxis means taking an antiviral before infection. Consistent users can reduce infection risk by over 70%; intermittent users gain little protection.

Explanation & sources ↗

Chapter 02

Avoid a slow decline

This chapter includes chronic risks with a large effect on overall mortality or strong evidence, ranked by cost-effectiveness. Randomized trials compare randomly assigned groups and provide the most reliable results here. Other figures come from observational studies that follow people without assigning treatments.

42 matching suggestions

02-01Evidence A

Quit smoking as early as possible

Smokers live more than ten years less on average than non-smokers. Quitting before 40 removes about 90% of the excess mortality risk from continuing. The earlier you quit, the more you regain.

Explanation & sources ↗
02-02Evidence A

Do not smoke at home or in the car, and do not let visitors smoke at home

Around 600,000 people worldwide die from secondhand smoke each year; nearly 30% are children. Long-term exposure raises hypertension, heart disease and stroke risks by roughly 30%.

Explanation & sources ↗
02-03Evidence A

Do not rely on willpower alone to quit smoking; medication can more than double success

Most people cannot quit by enduring cravings alone. Varenicline more than doubles cessation rates versus placebo. Nicotine patches or gum raise success by about 50% compared with no medication.

Explanation & sources ↗
02-04Evidence A

Set a quit date and stop completely that day instead of cutting down gradually

At six months, 22% of people who stopped abruptly on a planned date remained smoke-free, compared with 15.5% of those who gradually reduced their smoking.

Explanation & sources ↗
02-05Evidence A

Visit a smoking-cessation clinic or call China's 12320 service to ask about local support

Medication and regular follow-up are separate tools that work best together. Those receiving both were almost twice as likely to quit as people given only brief advice.

Explanation & sources ↗
02-06Evidence A

Consider e-cigarettes only if you cannot otherwise quit; non-smokers should avoid them

Switching to nicotine e-cigarettes produced about 60% more successful quits than nicotine patches, a well-supported finding. They are not harmless, and long-term safety data are still lacking.

Explanation & sources ↗
02-07Evidence A

Avoid sugary drinks; switching to sugar-free versions does not fully solve the problem

People drinking more than two bottles of sweet drinks daily had about 20% higher mortality during follow-up than those who rarely drank them. One to two bottles also meant an increase of over 10%.

Explanation & sources ↗
02-08Evidence A

Do not chew betel nut

Betel-nut users had about 20% higher mortality during follow-up and nearly 50% higher risks of diabetes and metabolic syndrome. Oral and esophageal cancer risks are additional.

Explanation & sources ↗
02-09Evidence A

Replace household salt with a low-sodium, potassium-containing salt

Among stroke survivors or people over 60 with hypertension, switching to low-sodium salt reduced five-year mortality by about 12% and stroke by about 14%.

Explanation & sources ↗
02-10Evidence B

Brush carefully, clean between teeth daily and replace missing teeth promptly

Daily floss or interdental-brush users had about 10% lower mortality during follow-up. Older adults with no teeth had about 90% higher mortality; those with fewer than 20 teeth had roughly twice the risk.

Explanation & sources ↗
02-11Evidence A

Aim for 7,000 to 8,000 steps a day

People taking 5,800 steps daily had about 40% lower mortality during follow-up than those taking 3,500. At 7,800 steps, the reduction was about 45%.

Explanation & sources ↗
02-12Evidence A

Take prescribed medication regularly for high blood pressure or cholesterol; do not stop on your own

Each 10 mmHg blood-pressure reduction cuts mortality by about 13% and stroke by about 27%. Lowering LDL cholesterol by one unit with statins reduces mortality by about 10%.

Explanation & sources ↗
02-13Evidence A

Sleep around seven hours each night on a regular schedule

Those consistently sleeping under seven hours had about 10% higher mortality during follow-up. Irregular schedules added risk; the most regular sleepers had 20% to nearly 50% lower risk than the least regular.

Explanation & sources ↗
02-14Evidence A

Accumulate 150 to 300 minutes of moderate exercise weekly; brisk walking is enough

Those brisk-walking 150 to 300 minutes weekly had about 30% lower mortality during follow-up than inactive people. Even less reduced it by 20%. At three to five times that amount, the reduction plateaued near 40%.

Explanation & sources ↗
02-15Evidence A

Play racket sports three times a week for 45 minutes each

Regular tennis, badminton or table-tennis players had roughly half the mortality during follow-up and 56% lower cardiovascular mortality than non-players. Swimmers had about 28% lower mortality.

Explanation & sources ↗
02-16Evidence A

Accumulate four or five minutes daily of vigorous everyday movement, such as stairs or fast walking

Otherwise inactive people doing three daily bursts of one or two minutes had about 40% lower mortality during follow-up and nearly half the cardiovascular mortality of those doing none.

Explanation & sources ↗
02-17Evidence A

Do 30 to 60 minutes of strength training each week

People strength-training 30 to 60 minutes weekly had 10% to 20% lower mortality during follow-up. More was not necessarily better; combining strength and aerobic exercise worked best.

Explanation & sources ↗
02-18Evidence A

Break up prolonged sitting by getting up and moving periodically

Those sitting the most had 2.6 times the mortality during follow-up of those sitting the least. Long uninterrupted sitting adds a separate risk.

Explanation & sources ↗
02-19Evidence A

Eat less processed meat, including ham, bacon, sausages and luncheon meat

Those eating the most processed meat had about 20% higher mortality during follow-up than those eating the least. An additional daily serving also raised risk by 20%.

Explanation & sources ↗
02-20Evidence A

Drink less alcohol or none

Above 100 g of pure alcohol weekly, higher consumption was linked to earlier death. That amount is roughly 2.5 liters of beer.

Explanation & sources ↗
02-21Evidence B

If you drink daily and get tremors or palpitations when stopping, do not quit without medical help

Abruptly stopping heavy daily drinking can cause withdrawal: tremors, sweating, palpitations and insomnia in milder cases, or seizures and delirium tremens in severe cases. These can be fatal emergencies.

Explanation & sources ↗
02-22Evidence A

To reduce drinking, count your weekly intake and discuss it briefly with a doctor

A few minutes reviewing intake, risks and a target with a doctor reduced average weekly consumption after one year by 20 g of alcohol, roughly half a liter of beer. Longer conversations offered no extra benefit.

Explanation & sources ↗
02-23Evidence A

Eat a small handful of nuts daily

Regular nut eaters had about 20% lower mortality during follow-up than non-eaters. Once weekly already showed about a 10% difference; a daily handful showed the strongest difference.

Explanation & sources ↗
02-24Evidence A

Replace some red meat with fish or poultry

Two additional weekly servings of processed or red meat were linked to about 3% higher mortality during follow-up. The same extra servings of fish or poultry showed no increase.

Explanation & sources ↗
02-25Evidence A

Replace some refined rice and flour with whole grains

An extra 90 g of whole grains daily was linked to about 17% lower mortality during follow-up. That is roughly three servings; the decline continued up to around 200 g daily.

Explanation & sources ↗
02-26Evidence A

Drink tea at least three times a week

Habitual tea drinkers had about 15% lower mortality during follow-up. From age 50, they averaged 1.26 extra years of life and 1.41 extra years free of cardiovascular disease.

Explanation & sources ↗
02-27Evidence A

Drink three to four cups of coffee daily without sugar or cream toppings

Those drinking three to four cups daily had about 17% lower mortality during follow-up than non-drinkers.

Explanation & sources ↗
02-28Evidence A

Eat five portions, around 400 g, of fruit and vegetables daily

Each additional 200 g daily was linked to about 10% lower mortality during follow-up. Five portions versus two meant around 13% lower mortality; more did not reduce it further.

Explanation & sources ↗
02-29Evidence A

Eat fewer ultra-processed foods, such as chips, instant noodles, pastries and ready meals

The highest consumers had about 20% higher mortality during follow-up and 50% higher cardiovascular mortality than the lowest. This evidence was rated uncertain, so treat the figures cautiously.

Explanation & sources ↗
02-30Evidence A

Use electricity or gas instead of coal or wood for cooking and heating

Coal or wood cooking was linked to about 10% higher mortality during follow-up, and heating with them to about 14% higher mortality. Those switching to electricity or gas had 13%–33… lower mortality than continuing users.

Explanation & sources ↗
02-31Evidence A

Let hot drinks cool; avoid scalding tea, soup and coffee

Very hot tea was linked to eight times the esophageal-cancer risk of warm tea; merely hot tea to twice the risk. Drinking within two minutes of pouring carried five times the risk of waiting at least four minutes.

Explanation & sources ↗
02-32Evidence B

Get some daylight outside rather than avoiding light all day

Women who deliberately avoided sunlight had 0.6 to 2.1 years less life expectancy than those with the most exposure. Sun-avoiding non-smokers had similar longevity to smokers with the most exposure.

Explanation & sources ↗
02-33Evidence A

Keep BMI around 20 to 25 and lose weight if overweight

Mortality risk was lowest at BMI 20 to 25. At 27.5 to 30 it was about 20% higher, at 30 to 35 about 45% higher, and at 35 to 40 nearly doubled.

Explanation & sources ↗
02-34Evidence B

Eat chili peppers at least four times a week

Those doing so had about 23% lower mortality during follow-up and roughly one-third lower cardiovascular mortality than those rarely eating chili.

Explanation & sources ↗
02-35Evidence B

Have one or two servings of milk or yogurt daily

Those having at least two servings daily had about 17% lower mortality during follow-up than those having none.

Explanation & sources ↗
02-36Evidence B

You need not avoid eggs, but do not eat three or four every day

Each additional half a whole egg daily was linked to about 7% higher mortality during follow-up. Replacing that half with egg whites, fish, poultry or nuts was linked to lower risks across causes of death.

Explanation & sources ↗
02-37Evidence B

Take baths if feasible rather than only showers

Near-daily bathers had about 28% lower cardiovascular-event risk and 46% lower cerebral-hemorrhage risk than those bathing fewer than twice weekly.

Explanation & sources ↗
02-38Evidence B

Keep naps under 30 minutes and avoid over an hour; investigate needing one or two hours to function

Naps under an hour showed no increase in mortality or chronic disease and somewhat better alertness. Longer naps were linked to about 30% more coronary disease and 20% more diabetes and obesity.

Explanation & sources ↗
02-39Evidence B

Catch up on lost sleep the next night instead of saving it for the weekend

Those not recovering lost sleep the following night had about 15% higher mortality risk than regular sleepers; severe shortfall without recovery meant about 42% higher risk. Recovery showed no detectable increase.

Explanation & sources ↗
02-40Evidence A

Longer night-shift work raises cardiovascular risk; switch roles early if possible

Night workers had about 13% more cardiovascular disease and 27% more cardiovascular deaths. Each additional five years of night shifts added roughly 7% more cardiovascular disease.

Explanation & sources ↗
02-41Evidence B

Buy packaged cooking oil with a Chinese SC production-license number; avoid unregulated bulk peanut oil

Damp, moldy peanuts can contain aflatoxin, an established carcinogen that mainly harms the liver. After Guangzhou regulated small oil workshops, abnormal liver function among regular users of self-pressed oil fell about 35%.

Explanation & sources ↗
02-42Evidence A

Use vegetable oil instead of lard or butter; rotating oils is unnecessary, and flaxseed oil is not proven heart protection

Replacing saturated fats such as lard and butter with vegetable oils reduced heart disease and stroke events by about 17%, but showed no detectable change in overall mortality.

Explanation & sources ↗

Chapter 03

Protect your energy and attention

This chapter counts energy and time: usable daily attention, reaction speed, mistakes and recovery after interruption. All figures are measured directly in experiments or studies following groups of people, known as cohort studies.

25 matching suggestions

03-01Evidence B

Turn off unnecessary notifications and keep your phone out of sight while working

A phone notification lowers attention-task performance even when you neither look at nor touch it. The effect is similar to actually taking a call or sending a message.

Explanation & sources ↗
03-02Evidence B

Wake up at the same time, including weekends

The least regular fifth of sleepers had body clocks about 2.5 hours later than the most regular fifth, effectively living with persistent jet lag. Students with more regular sleep schedules also had better grades.

Explanation & sources ↗
03-03Evidence A

Sleep seven to eight hours nightly; do not assume six is enough

Two weeks of six-hour nights brought cognitive performance down to the level of two nights without sleep. The problem is that people often do not notice the decline themselves.

Explanation & sources ↗
03-04Evidence A

Avoid caffeine after 2 p.m.

A large coffee containing 400 mg of caffeine six hours before bed reduced objectively measured sleep by over an hour. Participants' own sleep diaries did not detect the difference.

Explanation & sources ↗
03-05Evidence B

Batch email and messages at a few fixed times daily

The same people compared two weeks. In the week they checked email only three times daily, stress was noticeably lower despite sending and receiving the same number of messages.

Explanation & sources ↗
03-06Evidence B

Prevent even brief interruptions during work requiring continuous thought

An interruption averaging 2.8 seconds doubled the chance of an error in the next action. A 4.4-second interruption tripled it.

Explanation & sources ↗
03-07Evidence B

Do one thing at a time; do not answer messages during meetings

Switching tasks slows reactions and increases mistakes. Frequent multi-screen users had not developed better multitasking abilities; they performed worse on task-switching tests.

Explanation & sources ↗
03-08Evidence B

Avoid light-emitting screens for an hour before bed; choose paper or e-ink

Reading a lit screen before bed delayed sleep by about ten minutes versus paper, suppressed melatonin by 55%, and shifted the next day's body clock by over 1.5 hours, increasing morning sleepiness and recovery time.

Explanation & sources ↗
03-09Evidence B

Go to bed on time; do not stay up for games, short videos or pornography

In 2025, people in China averaged 6.97 hours of nighttime sleep and fell asleep at 00:10. Pre-bed phone or tablet users were more than twice as likely to get insufficient sleep, and their daytime-sleepiness risk was…

Explanation & sources ↗
03-10Evidence B

Avoid major decisions or important messages late at night

Well-rested people quickly learn to avoid high-risk choices. After two sleepless nights, they repeatedly choose risky options instead, especially at older ages.

Explanation & sources ↗
03-11Evidence B

If sleepy in the afternoon, nap for ten minutes rather than half an hour

A ten-minute nap improves alertness immediately for up to 2.5 hours. Five minutes has little effect; a 20-minute nap takes about half an hour to show benefits.

Explanation & sources ↗
03-12Evidence B

Use earplugs or a quiet room for memory-intensive work in an open-plan office

Increasing background noise from 39 to 51 decibels reduced word recall, increased fatigue and lowered motivation.

Explanation & sources ↗
03-13Evidence B

Keep weekly working hours below 49

Records from British munitions factories during World War I showed output proportional to hours up to 49 weekly. Beyond that, each extra hour produced progressively less additional work.

Explanation & sources ↗
03-14Evidence B

When you keep replaying the same upsetting event, switch to a hands-on task

Repetitive rumination does not produce an answer. It worsens depression, entrenches negative thoughts, impairs problem-solving and action, and can wear out people willing to listen…

Explanation & sources ↗
03-15Evidence B

Treat thoughts such as “things will definitely get worse” as symptoms, not facts

In a 20-year twin study, each increase in pessimism level was linked to about 13% higher mortality during follow-up and 20% higher cardiovascular mortality.

Explanation & sources ↗
03-16Evidence C

Reduce draining relationships and learn to decline unwanted requests

A draining person has a larger and more consistent negative effect than a supportive person's benefit. Remove sources of strain before adding support.

Explanation & sources ↗
03-17Evidence C

Standardize low-value decisions such as clothing and meals

This lacks strong evidence. The original finding that making choices depletes willpower failed to replicate in two large-scale studies.

Explanation & sources ↗
03-18Evidence B

Step away when angry; treat the other person like weather rather than an enemy

Reframing an event or taking the other person's perspective measurably reduces emotion, with perspective-taking more effective. Simply suppressing outward expression does not help.

Explanation & sources ↗
03-19Evidence A

When low, start with high-value actions: move, get daylight, sleep regularly, talk to someone or call China's 12356 helpline

For depression, brisk walking and jogging had the strongest effects, followed by yoga and strength training; higher intensity helped more. Light exposure works strongly for seasonal depression and also helps non-seasonal depression.

Explanation & sources ↗
03-20Evidence C

Treat police, doctors and bank staff as workers governed by procedures: documents and deadlines move matters forward, not emotion

These workers operate under role-specific rules, paperwork, deadlines and oversight. Their manner has little connection with whether your matter gets handled or how quickly.

Explanation & sources ↗
03-21Evidence A

Do not make comparing peers' lives a daily obligation; limit or disable those feeds

Habitually comparing yourself online with people doing better is linked to worse mood and lower self-esteem. Deactivating Facebook for four weeks slightly improved well-being but reduced knowledge of current events…

Explanation & sources ↗
03-22Evidence B

When you think everyone noticed your embarrassment, halve that estimate

People entering a room in an embarrassing T-shirt thought nearly half the observers could identify the person printed on it. In reality, fewer than a quarter could.

Explanation & sources ↗
03-23Evidence B

Treat “others expect me to be perfect” as a symptom, not a fact

People who feel others demand perfection and will reject them for falling short are more prone to suicidal thoughts. Self-imposed perfectionism has a much weaker link, only a third… of the former.

Explanation & sources ↗
03-24Evidence A

Do not vent anger by smashing things, punching bags or running; calm your body first

Activities that increase arousal, such as punching bags, smashing objects or running, do not generally reduce anger. Slow breathing, mindfulness and meditation noticeably reduce anger and the urge to act…

Explanation & sources ↗
03-25Evidence B

If something weighs on you, write your thoughts and feelings for several days, but do not expect a cure

Expressive writing has a small average benefit, but reviews disagree; two found no effect. It costs almost nothing and may be worth trying.

Explanation & sources ↗

Chapter 04

Protect your time

This chapter counts hours saved per day, week or year, or improvements in completing tasks on time. Time is not converted into lifespan or money. Where money is involved, a calculation method is provided rather than a universal conclusion.

18 matching suggestions

04-01Evidence A

Turn “I intend to” into a specific time, place and trigger for action

Replace “I will do this” with “At my desk at 8 a.m. Tuesday, I will start the introduction.” Across 94 tests, people using such plans achieved goals noticeably more often, a medium-to-large… effect.

Explanation & sources ↗
04-02Evidence B

Write exit conditions before starting

Write a rule such as “If this metric is not reached by this date, stop.” Combined studies show this helps people disengage from goals they cannot achieve.

Explanation & sources ↗
04-03Evidence B

Decide whether to continue using future costs and returns, not sunk costs

Money and time already invested make people more inclined to continue. Across 98 datasets, this tendency was consistent.

Explanation & sources ↗

Do not collect a serious diagnosis alone that week; postpone decisions unrelated to treatment

In the first week after cancer diagnosis, suicide risk was 12.6 times that of people without a diagnosis and cardiovascular mortality 5.6 times.

Explanation & sources ↗
29-03Evidence A

After unemployment, stabilize sleep routines, medical insurance and job-search rhythm rather than staying home all day

Subsequent mortality was about 60% higher than among employed people, especially men and younger people, highest in the first ten years.

Explanation & sources ↗
29-04Evidence A

After a relative dies by suicide, accident or homicide, seek professional help rather than simply enduring

Within five years after a spouse's suicide, diagnosed mental-disorder risk was about 80% higher for men and 70% for women than the general population, and 70% to 100% higher than after other spousal deaths.

Explanation & sources ↗
29-05Evidence A

For the first six months of widowhood, assign someone to check meals, sleep, chronic medication and reviews

Mortality during follow-up was about 40% higher in the first six months, dropping to 15% higher afterward. Men showed about 23% higher risk; the female estimate was small enough to be chance.

Explanation & sources ↗
29-06Evidence B

Without family or friends, arrange a neighbor with access, community visits and phone emergency contacts

Ensure someone can discover an emergency and that meals and medication happen regularly. Use written lists and alarms rather than memory for the latter.

Explanation & sources ↗
29-07Evidence B

After a parent's death, tell children truthfully and let them participate in farewell; do not send them away merely for a change of scene

Losing a parent before 18 was linked to about 50% higher early-adult mortality; accidental or suicidal deaths to about 80% higher, illness deaths to about 30% higher.

Explanation & sources ↗
29-08Evidence A

If grief remains disabling after six months, seek psychiatry or clinical psychology

About one in ten bereaved adults remains stuck, with prolonged longing preventing eating, work or childcare, numbness and a sense that life lacks meaning.

Explanation & sources ↗
29-09Evidence A

Do not immediately pay for grief counseling; first check for the persistent symptoms in entry eight

Counseling all bereaved people has only small, short-lived benefits because most recover naturally.

Explanation & sources ↗
29-10Evidence A

After separation or divorce, keep medical insurance and do not cope through alcohol

Premature mortality is higher than among still-married people, especially men and younger adults. This may reflect pre-existing health or income differences rather than divorce causing it…

Explanation & sources ↗
29-11Evidence B

For someone to talk to, call China's 12356; minors and young people can call 12355, while medical care uses a mental-health clinic

The national 12356 psychological-assistance hotline is free. The 12355 youth service provides another route for minors and young people.

Explanation & sources ↗
29-12Evidence C

Postpone irreversible major decisions during the first three months after a crisis

Judgment of opportunities is poorest then. Claims of contacting the deceased, recovering lost money, relocating for a new start or joining business partnerships may target you.

Explanation & sources ↗
29-13Evidence A

Death is not a way to repay debts: early-policy suicide does not pay life insurance, work-injury benefits do not apply and debts still reduce the estate

Suicide within a life policy's first two years does not trigger the death benefit, only refundable policy value. It is not a work injury, so the three death-at-work payments are absent. Debts are paid from the estate first.

Explanation & sources ↗

Chapter 30

Children after starting school

Chapter 20 covers the first year, and chapter 18 the money and time of parenting. This chapter covers the intervening years from three to 18.

15 matching suggestions

30-01Evidence A

For sudden severe and worsening pain, take the child to hospital immediately rather than waiting for school to end

Some conditions depend on hours. Sudden one-sided scrotal pain may be testicular torsion, twisting the blood supply and cutting it off.

Explanation & sources ↗
30-02Evidence A

Do not delay needed treatment until exams finish; some windows depend on bone age, not school schedules

Scoliosis bends the spine sideways. A rigid brace while bones grow kept 75% of children from reaching surgical severity; among those merely observed, only…

Explanation & sources ↗
30-03Evidence A

Report bullying to school that day and demand written handling; report assault, robbery or rumor-spreading to police

Bullied children had about 2.2 times the suicidal-thought risk and 2.6 times the suicidal-behavior risk of non-bullied children.

Explanation & sources ↗
30-04Evidence A

Aim for two hours outdoors daily; the source describes this as the only myopia-prevention method supported by randomized trials

Adding 40 minutes of daily outdoor lessons in first grade reduced new myopia over three years from about 40% to about 30%.

Explanation & sources ↗
30-05Evidence B

No screens under three, minimize at three to six, and keep non-study use under one hour daily for schoolchildren

China's health guidance also limits schoolchildren's individual non-study sessions to 15 minutes.

Explanation & sources ↗
30-06Evidence A

Treat myopia as lasting damage: greater severity means more later retinal detachment, macular disease and glaucoma

Myopia does not simply resolve or reverse, and is more than needing glasses. Even mild myopia carried over ten times the myopic-macular-disease risk; above six diopters…

Explanation & sources ↗
30-07Evidence B

Read annual school health reports yourself and investigate abnormalities that year

Reports particularly flag overweight, obesity, malnutrition, abnormal spinal curvature, poor vision and dental decay, all easily neglected.

Explanation & sources ↗
30-08Evidence B

Screen ages 12 to 18 for depression; a school psychological questionnaire is not a diagnosis

US preventive guidance supports major-depression screening at 12 to 18; evidence under 12 is insufficient. Suicide is the second leading cause of death at ages ten to 19.

Explanation & sources ↗
30-09Evidence B

Do not buy products or services claiming to cure myopia or reduce prescriptions

China's market regulator states current medical technology cannot cure myopia and targets claims of recovery, reduced degree, cure or prescription repair.

Explanation & sources ↗
30-10Evidence B

Sleep, homework, physical education and ranking have explicit school rules; raise noncompliance

Guidance specifies ten hours' sleep for primary pupils, nine for junior-high and eight for senior-high students. Classes generally start no earlier than 8:20 in primary school or 8:00 in secondary school.

Explanation & sources ↗
30-11Evidence B

A struggling child can take formal leave while retaining enrollment, up to one year per application

Parents or guardians apply, the school confirms and higher authorities approve. Further leave requires a new application after expiry.

Explanation & sources ↗
30-12Evidence B

For poor vision, obtain hospital cycloplegic refraction and follow advised review intervals

Eye drops relax focusing muscles before measuring the prescription. This is performed in hospital and provides the most accurate myopia diagnosis.

Explanation & sources ↗
30-13Evidence A

Seal the grooves after permanent molars erupt

Resin seals chewing-surface grooves against food debris. After two years, decay risk was about one eighth that without sealing.

Explanation & sources ↗
30-14Evidence B

For gaming, check whether sleep, homework and outdoor activity are displaced rather than only hours played

About two or three people per hundred meet gaming-disorder criteria. Low questionnaire thresholds or adolescent-only samples can inflate estimates.

Explanation & sources ↗
30-15Evidence B

If a child says they are attracted to the same sex, do not insult, expel or send them for conversion; family attitudes relate to suicide risk

Among Chinese secondary students, same-sex or bisexual attraction was linked to about three to 5.5 times the annual suicide-attempt rate of others.

Explanation & sources ↗

Chapter 31

Routes after turning 18

This chapter counts money and time, with refusal of military service also affecting freedom. It is a map rather than a full manual: statutory entry requirements, military benefits, public-sector routes beyond civil-service exams, university choices…

16 matching suggestions

31-01Evidence A

Compare entry requirements first: age and education for twelve routes are explicitly prescribed

Employment starts at 16. Male military enlistment starts at 18, with the maximum age extended to 24 for bachelor's graduates.

Explanation & sources ↗
31-02Evidence A

Complete military registration by October 31 in the year you turn 18; conscript active service lasts two years

Registration is a legal duty, not an enlistment application or a commitment to serve. Men turning 18 that year must complete it online before October 31.

Explanation & sources ↗
31-03Evidence A

Refusing service after enlistment brings two-year exit and education restrictions and exclusion from civil-service and state-sector jobs

Civil service, state enterprises and public institutions cannot recruit you. For two years, overseas travel, further study and returning to school are barred under the source's account.

Explanation & sources ↗
31-04Evidence A

For university students, key military benefits include tuition support up to 20,000 yuan yearly, two-year enrollment retention and special postgraduate admissions

Current students, new graduates and incoming students receive tuition support during service: up to 20,000 yuan annually for undergraduate/junior-college students and 25,000 for postgraduates…

Explanation & sources ↗
31-05Evidence A

Only six situations receive government job placement after discharge; self-employed-route veterans must report within 30 days

Guaranteed placement is not universal. Most two-year conscripts do not fall within the six qualifying categories.

Explanation & sources ↗
31-06Evidence A

Count three post-service benefits: a one-off retirement payment, service counted as employment years and up to 20,000 yuan annual business-tax relief

The first is the one-off payment for the self-employment route, based on active-service years with additional amounts for meritorious service.

Explanation & sources ↗
31-07Evidence A

Public-sector routes include grassroots service: two qualifying years open targeted recruitment comprising 10% of annual plans

Projects such as teaching, agriculture, health and poverty support enable eligible graduates after two years and satisfactory assessment to enter targeted recruitment.

Explanation & sources ↗
31-08Evidence A

Special-post teachers completing three satisfactory years and wishing to stay should receive established posts promptly

Eligibility centers on bachelor's education, mainly teacher-training majors, age no more than 30 and the relevant teaching qualification.

Explanation & sources ↗
31-09Evidence A

Firefighting and military civilian recruitment provide other public routes with lower entry barriers

Neither universally requires junior-college education. Firefighters recruit ages 18 to 22 with senior-high education; college graduates and veterans may qualify up to 24…

Explanation & sources ↗
31-10Evidence A

Education is not a one-time chance: self-study exams, adult entrance exams and open universities offer later routes

Self-study exams have no age or prior-education limits under the source's account, though full-time enrolled students cannot apply. Adult examinations and open universities are other formal channels.

Explanation & sources ↗
31-11Evidence A

Independent work means flexible employment: arrange pension and health insurance yourself at the work location

There is no employer paying the other share. Policy calls for lifting household-registration restrictions for flexible-worker insurance, with some megacities allowed gradual implementation.

Explanation & sources ↗
31-12Evidence A

For delivery, ride-hailing and local freight, platforms pay occupational-injury protection per order, not workers

Each order receives coverage and the worker contributes nothing personally.

Explanation & sources ↗
31-13Evidence A

Two university choices can secure public posts: state-funded teacher education and targeted medicine, in exchange for six years' service

The state funds study, and graduates serve at designated locations for six years. State-funded teacher programs recruit in the early admissions round at six ministry-affiliated teacher universities.

Explanation & sources ↗
31-14Evidence A

For overseas work, verify the organizer's foreign-labor-cooperation license; it may not charge a deposit

Only qualified, registered enterprises may organize overseas labor under China's rules.

Explanation & sources ↗
31-15Evidence A

Remote work from China for foreign firms is domestic-source income: declare tax yourself and receive funds as employee compensation

Source follows where the work occurs, not where payment originates. Working remotely from China creates income taxable there.

Explanation & sources ↗
31-16Evidence A

For borrowed startup capital, first check guaranteed startup loans: up to 300,000 yuan and half the interest subsidized

Individual loans can reach 300,000 yuan for up to three years, with government paying half the interest.

Explanation & sources ↗

Chapter 32

Studying abroad: status, work, insurance and degree recognition

This chapter counts money and personal freedom, without judging whether to go or comparing schools. Know how to maintain visa status, work-hour caps, mandatory insurance and charges, and whether the degree can be recognized on return.

10 matching suggestions

32-01Evidence A

Before paying tuition, check the school against China's overseas-degree-recognition institution lists

Using the degree for civil-service exams, state enterprises, household registration or professional titles requires recognition by the Chinese Service Center for Scholarly Exchange.

Explanation & sources ↗
32-02Evidence A

Follow litigation over US F-1 changes: the proposed four-year limit and 30-day departure rule, due September 15, 2026, were paused the day before; the source reports duration-of-study status remains

The US proposal would cap status at four years and require departure within 30 days after completion. A federal court paused it the day before its scheduled start.

Explanation & sources ↗
32-03Evidence A

Student work caps in the US, Canada, UK and Australia are hard visa limits; even one extra hour violates conditions

Exceeding limits can lead to visa cancellation, removal and questions on later applications.

Explanation & sources ↗
32-04Evidence A

Full-time enrollment underpins work permission; leave, withdrawal and gaps during transfers remove it

Work eligibility disappears on leave, withdrawal, expulsion or periods without classes during transfer. Continuing work then is unlawful under the described conditions.

Explanation & sources ↗
32-05Evidence A

In the US, report a new address within ten days of moving

Failure is itself unlawful and also risks missing immigration correspondence.

Explanation & sources ↗
32-06Evidence A

Check China's education-ministry study-abroad alerts before departure and while enrolled

These warn about recent safety or policy conditions unfavorable to Chinese students in specific destinations.

Explanation & sources ↗
32-07Evidence A

In Australia, OSHC must cover the full stay without gaps; absent proof on arrival may lead to entry refusal

Overseas Student Health Cover is a visa condition, not optional. Renewals or insurer changes must leave no coverage gap.

Explanation & sources ↗
32-08Evidence A

UK students pay an annual health surcharge of £776 in addition to visa fees, paid upfront

The source's rate means a two-year visa requires £1,552 upfront to access the National Health Service.

Explanation & sources ↗
32-09Evidence A

Allow ten to 20 working days for degree recognition before returning

That is review time alone. Recruitment peaks or returned documents can make it longer.

Explanation & sources ↗
32-10Evidence A

The list of schools under enhanced scrutiny grows; buying a diploma is no longer a viable route

China's recognition center names institutions for enhanced scrutiny and suspends applications from some schools.

Chapter 33

Living with disability

Prevention is in chapters one and 13. This chapter treats distinct measures separately: mortality for emergencies and complications, money for benefits and litigation, and time for education and administrative tasks, without converting them into one another.

20 matching suggestions

33-01Evidence B

After spinal-cord injury, sudden severe headache and sweating require sitting upright, loosening clothing and calling 120

Disrupted warning pathways mean a full bladder or tight clothing may go unnoticed while blood pressure surges. Sudden headache and sweating are signals.

Explanation & sources ↗
33-02Evidence A

The first ten years after disability carry elevated suicide risk; do not dismiss it as needing a better attitude

Emotional collapse in the person or family is common and not a willpower failure. Long follow-up at two UK spinal-injury centers found five times the general-population suicide rate.

Explanation & sources ↗
33-03Evidence A

Psychiatric admission is generally voluntary; only two situations permit admission without the person's consent

A relative's or employer's request alone is insufficient. The cited law permits it for actual or threatened self-harm, or actual or threatened harm to others.

Explanation & sources ↗
33-04Evidence A

Someone should monitor the health of the family member providing long-term care

Caregiver exhaustion is real. A US study followed over 800 older adults for four years; strained carers of disabled spouses had higher mortality than non-carers. The concise PDF truncates the size of the increase at “six…”.

Explanation & sources ↗
33-05Evidence B

For long-term wheelchair use, choose pressure-relieving cushions and inspect sitting bones and tailbone daily

Ordinary foam can cause slow-healing, infection-prone skin injury. Nursing-home pressure-relief cushions reduced sitting-bone ulcers, though including tailbone ulcers removed a detectable overall difference…

Explanation & sources ↗
33-06Evidence A

Do not buy therapies or devices promising to cure paralysis, blindness or deafness

Medical, drug and device advertising may not guarantee outcomes, state cure or success rates, or use testimonials under China's advertising law.

Explanation & sources ↗
33-07Evidence A

After obtaining a disability certificate, ask the county federation about all eligible applications

The certificate itself pays nothing; it unlocks separate benefits, each requiring its own application rather than automatic delivery.

Explanation & sources ↗
33-08Evidence A

For children under seven with disabilities or autism, apply for rehabilitation assistance

China's age-zero-to-six scheme covers surgery, assistive devices and rehabilitation training through county disability federations.

Explanation & sources ↗
33-09Evidence B

Apply to county-level or higher governments for home-ramp, handrail and bathroom adaptations

The accessibility law requires support and guidance for household adaptations and appropriate subsidies for eligible disabled and older households.

Explanation & sources ↗
33-10Evidence A

Tell prospective employers you hold a disability certificate; hiring you can offset a levy

The required employment proportion is at least 1.5% of staff, with the exact local ratio set by the province.

Explanation & sources ↗
33-11Evidence A

Disability may reduce personal income tax; ask the provincial tax authority about amounts

National law permits reductions but leaves amount and duration to provincial governments, so rules differ.

Explanation & sources ↗
33-12Evidence A

Assistance dogs can enter public venues and transport; blind people have free local public transport

Law calls for access for guide, hearing and assistance dogs. Valid credentials allow free urban buses, metro and ferries for blind people; disabled people may carry… free of charge.

Explanation & sources ↗
33-13Evidence A

Disabled university-entrance candidates can request accommodations; Braille papers allow 50% extra time

Options include Braille or large print, listening-test exemption, separate rooms, hearing aids, wheelchairs and extended time.

Explanation & sources ↗
33-14Evidence A

Schools may not reject eligible disabled children; education authorities arrange home teaching when attendance is impossible

Kindergartens, schools and ordinary vocational schools must accept eligible applicants with disabilities.

Explanation & sources ↗
33-15Evidence A

Loss or impairment of one or both lower limbs can still permit a C5 driving license

Applicants who can sit steadily and meet upper-limb requirements may qualify for adapted automatic cars. People missing one palm can also apply.

Explanation & sources ↗
33-16Evidence A

Use licensed rehabilitation departments and follow the therapist's intensity plan; harder is not always better

Taking someone home to wait passively is a common mistake. Organized multidisciplinary stroke care increased one-year survival and the chance of living at home.

Explanation & sources ↗
33-17Evidence A

Get hearing aids for hearing improvement, not as proven dementia prevention

A three-year trial of nearly 1,000 people found no overall difference establishing the dementia-prevention claim.

Explanation & sources ↗
33-18Evidence A

Only a court can declare an adult unable or partly unable to manage civil affairs; family cannot decide alone

Relatives, employers and neighborhood committees cannot independently make such a legal determination.

Explanation & sources ↗
33-19Evidence A

Adult guardians follow the statutory order; guardians may compensate when the person harms others

The sequence is spouse, parents and children, other close relatives, then other willing people or organizations.

Explanation & sources ↗
33-20Evidence A

Disability-based rejection, withheld permanent status or underpayment can be challenged, but count the process costs

Discrimination is prohibited in hiring, regularization, promotion, titles, pay and social insurance. You may complain to the responsible authority or sue.

Chapter 34

Using household medicines safely

Fever, pain, cold, stomach and diarrhea medicines are often sold without prescriptions, but that does not make every use safe. This chapter covers simple actions avoiding serious consequences rather than prescribing for each disease.

9 matching suggestions

34-01Evidence B

Before combining cold or pain medicines, check ingredients; only one should contain paracetamol/acetaminophen

Many cold remedies contain it, so two boxes can double the dose and harm the liver. In US acute liver failure caused by it, nearly 30% died before transplantation.

Explanation & sources ↗
34-02Evidence B

Do not use aspirin, nimesulide or metamizole for children's fever, or metamizole-containing cold medicines for minors

Aspirin is linked to Reye syndrome affecting brain and liver. About 30% of affected US children died; cases fell by over 90% after warnings.

Explanation & sources ↗
34-03Evidence A

Ask a doctor before ibuprofen-like painkillers if over 60, with prior stomach bleeding, or taking anticoagulants or steroids

Ibuprofen, naproxen and aspirin can harm the stomach. High-dose trials found about four times the bleeding or perforation risk with ibuprofen versus none.

Explanation & sources ↗
34-04Evidence B

Do not self-administer combination cold or cough medicines to children under two

China's drug regulator required warnings on 14 pediatric combination cold products advising use only under doctor or pharmacist guidance for this age.

Explanation & sources ↗
34-05Evidence B

Do not self-administer ibuprofen-like painkillers after 20 weeks of pregnancy

Most amniotic fluid then comes from fetal kidneys. These drugs can damage those kidneys and reduce fluid.

Explanation & sources ↗
34-06Evidence B

Limit self-bought omeprazole for heartburn to seven days; swallowing difficulty, vomiting blood or black stools require hospital care

Enteric-coated tablets became non-prescription in China in 2022, but instructions limit self-use to seven days and prohibit another course within two months.

Explanation & sources ↗
34-07Evidence A

Do not ask for antibiotics for an ordinary cold

They do not speed recovery, while adult adverse-effect risk more than doubles. Purulent nasal discharge under ten days also has no established benefit from antibiotics.

Explanation & sources ↗
34-08Evidence A

For diarrhea, prioritize oral rehydration salts; do not give antidiarrheals to under-fives

Hydration matters more than stopping stools. Mix salts as instructed; juice is not a substitute because excess sugar can worsen dehydration.

Explanation & sources ↗
34-09Evidence B

Do not use simple painkillers over 15 days monthly or combination ones over ten; they may be causing the headaches

Daily painkillers for recurrent headache can worsen it. International classification calls this medication-overuse headache.

Explanation & sources ↗
